The two-word name fits the alliteration clue perfectly, and it aligns with Vonnegut’s habit of pulling from biblical or hagiographic sources in his commentary on art and suffering.

Current working hypothesis remains Pablo Picasso PP, with James Joyce JJ as strongest conceptual runner-up acknowledged but no active defender in round 4, and persistent minority iconographic proposal Saint Stephen SS.

Round 4 public positions: 8 colleagues endorse Pablo Picasso – 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 – all invoking Vonnegut’s photographic-type constancy gag: “in all the pictures” = a public figure visually frozen by portraiture then reduced to a one-line animal simile. Support emphasizes Picasso’s famously invariant late-life studio/press record 1930s-1960s, white spiky quill-like hair and gaunt bristly beard essentially identical picture to picture, mapping cleanly to porcupine simile and PP alliteration. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 all keep Joyce JJ as the strongest credible visual/hair-quill runner-up on same photographic constancy logic and perfect alliteration, but note Joyce now has no active defender after round 3.

Saint Stephen SS held by Colleagues 7 and 10 in round 4. They argue clue aligns with Vonnegut’s documented use of stylized suffering/hagiographic imagery, medieval/Renaissance depictions of Stephen encircled by halo of stones/arrows producing bristling porcupine silhouette, and that Vonnegut routinely merges stylized religious sources with modern commentary. They claim Picasso/Joyce endorsements rest on un-sourced “in all the pictures” claim never tied to Palm Sunday, interviews or letters, and that Vonnegut preferred hagiographic sources over twentieth-century snapshots. Counter from Picasso camp: that reading shifts “in all the pictures” from photographic record to iconographic depiction, breaking literal photographic framing Vonnegut uses for modern artist/writer porcupine gag, and no verbatim Vonnegut porcupine-in-every-picture citation for Stephen is offered.

Important preserved claims/evidence:
- Picasso supporters stress independent repetition across rounds 0-1-2-3-4, 8-way support in round 4, photographic invariance 1940s-1960s.
- Joyce supporters historically stressed bristly standing-up hair/moustache present in virtually every portrait, perfect JJ alliteration, writer-canon context, same photographic constancy logic.
- Stephen supporters stress repeated martyr halo of stones/arrows, Vonnegut’s essays on suffering and hagiographic references, SS alliteration fits.

Disagreements unresolved:
Photographic constancy vs iconographic reading of “in all the pictures”; whether Vonnegut’s porcupine gag is confined to modern portraiture or extends to stylised religious art; whether lack of primary citation invalidates Picasso/Joyce.

Changes in belief: frequency moved decisively to Picasso, loss of active Joyce defender reduces its current public weight though colleagues still acknowledge it as best conceptual alternative. Saint Stephen remains minority but consistent at 2 votes.

Unresolved core remains: no primary Vonnegut source with exact wording “looks like a porcupine in all the pictures” has been produced by any colleague. Needed from Palm Sunday, interviews, letters, essays to close Picasso vs Joyce definitively and to rule out Stephen. Current belief: stronger provisional Pablo Picasso on frequency + visual-photographic fit + alliterative match, pending verbatim primary citation.
reflection_text.2:
The candidate set remains Picasso PP, Saint Stephen SS and the withdrawn conceptual runner-up James Joyce JJ; Whitman WW, Reagan RR and Hesse HH are abandoned after Round 1.

Round 4 public positions are unchanged from Round 3: Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 endorse Pablo Picasso; Colleagues 7 and 10 endorse Saint Stephen. Joyce has no active defender in Round 4. Colleague 6 remains Picasso after his Round 2 switch Joyce→Picasso.

Picasso case as restated in Round 4:
* Vonnegut photographic-type constancy gag: “in all the pictures” = a public figure visually frozen by portraiture and reduced to a one-line animal simile.
* Late-life studio/press record 1930s-1960s is famously invariant: white spiky/quill-like hair and gaunt bristly beard essentially identical picture after picture.
* That unchanging spiky head maps cleanly onto porcupine simile and meets the required two-word alliteration P P.
* Independent repetition advantage persists: eight of ten colleagues in Round 4, 8-2 over Saint Stephen, with Colleague 6’s prior switch reinforcing stability.
* James Joyce JJ remains the strongest conceptual runner-up on bristly hair/moustache photographic constancy and perfect alliteration, but is now a holdover with zero current public support.

Saint Stephen case as restated by 7 and 10 in Round 4:
* Iconographic/thematic reading: Vonnegut’s documented use of religious martyrdom/hagiographic imagery; Stephen shown encircled by stones/arrows producing a bristling/porcupine silhouette.
* Claims the “looks like a porcupine in all the pictures” phrasing aligns with repeated medieval/Renaissance visual formula Vonnegut favored on suffering, and that Vonnegut routinely merges stylized religious sources with modern commentary rather than limiting the gag to twentieth-century snapshots.
* Alliteration SS satisfied.
* Critique of Picasso: the invariant portrait record has never been tied to the precise Vonnegut wording in Palm Sunday, interview, letter or essay; photographic claims rest on visual resemblance alone and Vonnegut’s preference for hagiographic sources is allegedly overlooked.

Counter to Saint Stephen from Picasso majority in Round 4:
* Shifts “in all the pictures” from photographic record to medieval/Renaissance hagiographic depiction; reading is projectile silhouette / iconography, not “looks the same in every picture” photographic constancy.
* No verbatim Vonnegut porcupine-in-every-picture citation produced for Stephen, and photographic framing of the clue is decisive against the iconographic reading.

Unresolved lock unchanged: no primary Vonnegut citation – Palm Sunday, interview, letter or essay – with the exact “looks like a porcupine in all the pictures” wording tied to a name has been produced in Rounds 0-4. Colleague 10 explicitly notes lack of documented phrase; Colleague 7 argues photographic objection is weaker because Vonnegut merges stylized sources.

Current working leaning remains Picasso PP due to multiplicity of independent advocates 8 of 10 in Round 4, best match to photographic constancy framing and alliterative fit. Saint Stephen is minority iconographic interpretation struggling with the photographic wording; Joyce is effectively withdrawn after Colleague 6’s switch but remains the closest alternative hypothesis if a primary source emerged.

reflection_text.8:
The question is for a two-word alliterative name Vonnegut described as looking like a porcupine “in all the pictures”, with emphasis on photographic constancy / visual freeze.

Round 0 baseline remains: Pablo Picasso P P – white/spiky hair and gaunt face, photographic type frozen in every studio/press portrait, 3 initial endorsements. James Joyce J J – bristly standing-up hair and moustache present in virtually every portrait, porcupine-like, 2 endorsements. Saint Stephen S S – religious/martyr iconography with stones/projectiles read as porcupine-like silhouette; iconographic not photographic, 2 endorsements. Walt Whitman W W, Ronald Reagan R R, Herman Hesse H H – singletons with spiky-hair anecdotes, no clear repeated Vonnegut citation.

Round 1-3 consolidation: Picasso now has Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 explicitly endorsing in Round 3 and staying in Round 4, citing photographic-type gag, unchanging white quill-like hair/beard 1930s-60s, classic Vonnegut aside about public figure reduced to single visual gag. Alliteration P P satisfied. Joyce collapsed to acknowledged runner-up only; Colleague 6 switched from Joyce/Hesse to Picasso in Round 2 and stays with Picasso in Round 4, still noting Joyce as closest visual runner-up on hair/quill logic and photographic constancy and perfect alliteration. No active Joyce champion in Round 3/4 public responses.
Saint Stephen held by Colleagues 7 and 10 in Rounds 3-4. Colleague 10 argues iconographic thread Vonnegut favored, projectile halo = porcupine silhouette, photographic claims un-sourced. Colleague 7 argues Vonnegut routinely blends stylized religious art with modern commentary, photographic objection does not hold, and Picasso/Joyce lack primary source.

Round 4 public positions:
Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 stay with Picasso, stress photographic-type constancy gag, unchanging spiky/quill hair, frequency and visual fit. All continue to note Joyce J J remains strongest alternative/runner-up on hair/quill logic and photographic constancy and perfect alliteration.
Colleague 10 and Colleague 7 hold Saint Stephen. Colleague 10 argues iconographic thread, projectile halo = porcupine silhouette, photographic claims un-sourced, Picasso record never tied to precise Vonnegut wording in Palm Sunday/interviews/letters. Persistent disagreements:
Photographic constancy vs iconography. Picasso camp says “in all the pictures” means photographic record; Saint Stephen camp says it means repeated artistic depictions with projectiles.
Writer canon vs artist canon. Joyce was framed as writer-focused; majority frames as artist-focused Picasso.
Evidence quality. No primary Vonnegut source cited in any round; all claims inferential from Vonnegut’s habit of visual animal similes. Lack of verifiable Palm Sunday/interview/letter citation remains key blocker.

Picasso is dominant hypothesis by frequency 7-2 in Round 4 and visual fit to “porcupine in all the pictures” photographic-type joke. A primary Vonnegut text confirming exact “porcupine in all the pictures” wording and name attached to it to break Picasso vs Joyce tie. Without it case remains inferential and open to Saint Stephen iconographic reading.
reflection_text.9:
Working hypothesis remains Pablo Picasso P P, with James Joyce J J as the closest conceptual runner-up and Saint Stephen S S as the minority iconographic alternative.

The question is framed as Vonnegut’s photographic-type constancy gag: “looks like a porcupine in all the pictures” / “looks the same in every picture” applied to a public figure visually frozen by portraiture and reduced to a one-line animal simile. The formal requirement is a two-word alliterative male name.

Picasso support now 8-way in R4, colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 staying with Pablo Picasso. Core claim: late-life studio and press record 1930s-1960s is famously invariant – white spiky/quill-like hair and gaunt bristly beard essentially identical picture after picture. That unchanging quilled head maps cleanly onto porcupine simile and satisfies P P alliteration. The phrasing “in all the pictures” is taken as literal photographic constancy, the mechanics Vonnegut repeatedly uses for modern artists/writers.

James Joyce J J is universally acknowledged as the strongest visual/photographic runner-up on the same bristly hair/moustache photographic constancy logic and perfect JJ alliteration. Colleagues keep Joyce as the credible alternative to move to if a primary Palm Sunday/interview/letter citation for the exact “porcupine in all the pictures” wording cannot be produced for Picasso. No active Joyce defender in R3-R4, though it remains the agreed best backup.

Saint Stephen S S is held by Colleagues 7 and 10 only. Argument: Vonnegut’s essays on suffering/stylized imagery favor hagiographic sources; Stephen is repeatedly shown in medieval/Renaissance art encircled by a halo of stones/arrows producing a bristling porcupine-like silhouette, a concrete recurrent referent. They claim Picasso/Joyce photographic claims are unsourced, never tied to precise Vonnegut wording in Palm Sunday/interviews/letters, and overlook Vonnegut’s documented preference for hagiographic material.

Counter to Stephen: shifts “in all the pictures” from photographic record to stylized hagiographic depiction; the motif is a projectile halo, not Vonnegut’s “looks the same in every picture” photographic gag for modern artists/writers; no verbatim Vonnegut porcupine-in-every-picture citation produced for Stephen.

Unresolved and critical: no primary Vonnegut text/interview/letter with exact “looks like a porcupine in all the pictures” wording for any candidate has been surfaced. The case for Picasso over Joyce rests on frequency of independent advocacy ~8 vs 0 active defenders and visual-photographic fit, not on a verified citation. If sourcing fails, Joyce is the only alternative that preserves the photographic constancy framing and perfect alliteration. Saint Stephen remains suspect relative to photographic framing, though Colleagues 7/10 insist Vonnegut blends stylized religious art with modern commentary and that the iconographic thread has been under-weighted.

Earlier R0-R3 dynamics preserved: Picasso gained from R0 3 endorsements to 8-way dominance; Joyce dropped from R0 2 endorsements to runner-up status; Saint Stephen persists 2-way from R0; Whitman, Reagan, Hesse dropped after R1. Colleague 6’s earlier switch from Hesse/Joyce to Picasso on frequency grounds remains relevant.

Current belief: Picasso best supported working hypothesis pending verbatim source, Joyce best fallback, Saint Stephen unlikely under literal photographic reading.
